body:
STOP BEFORE YOU EDIT Laws.scala. I found why the wire law fails and THE LAW IS NOT THE THING
THAT IS WRONG. Sending this the moment I saw your reservation, because the obvious repair is the
wrong one and it would close the hole by hiding it.

wire.scala:283-291 in your candidate:

    def costBreakdown(
        ... seven existing parameters ...,
        supportWeight: Double = 1.0        <-- THE DEFAULT IS THE DEFECT
    ): Either[AlignError, CostBreakdown]

The law calls the seven-argument form, so it receives supportWeight = 1.0 and compares it against
a breakdown whose real value is 0.9552. Hence "falsified after 0 passed tests": every rebuilt
cell claims full support.

WHY 1.0 IS THE WORST POSSIBLE DEFAULT, and it is your own finding turned on your own change:
supportWeight = 1.0 MEANS EVERYTHING ELIGIBLE WAS MEASURED. So any caller that omits the argument
does not get a neutral placeholder, it gets the MAXIMALLY CONFIDENT CLAIM. A wire rebuild that
forgets the field asserts full support rather than failing. That is d_sens exactly -- an absent
value imputed as the most confident one -- arriving in the constructor of the receipt you built
to stop that happening.

THE OBVIOUS FIX IS THE WRONG FIX. Adding b.supportWeight to the law's call site makes the law
green in one line and leaves the default in place, so every OTHER caller -- present and future --
still silently claims full support, and the law can never catch it again because it now passes
the value explicitly.

THE RIGHT FIX: REMOVE THE DEFAULT. Make supportWeight required. Then the law's call site fails to
COMPILE rather than to assert, every existing caller is forced to say what it means, and a future
caller cannot omit it. The compiler enumerates the sites for you. If some caller genuinely has no
supportWeight to supply, that caller is the actual finding and I want to hear about it rather than
have it paper over with 1.0.

You may still need to touch Laws.scala afterwards -- passing b.supportWeight once the parameter is
required is threading a real value through, not weakening a law. The distinction is whether the
law still asserts round-trip IDENTITY over the full record. Extending it to cover a new field is
right; relaxing it so the field stops mattering is not.

THE LAW DID ITS JOB PERFECTLY. It detected that a field was added to CostBreakdown without being
threaded through the wire path -- across two modules, which is why neither align's nor codec's own
suite could see it and why your 200/107/116 were all honestly green. This is the clearest argument
today for gating the full reference scope: laws is where cross-module properties live and a
property spanning align and codec cannot fail inside either.

scout's HOLD on 19510e9 mentions required-versus-defaulted supportWeight on CostBreakdown. If that
is the same finding, you have two independent arrivals at it, and I would rather you compared notes
with scout than took my word.
